prompt: Some cities offer free public transportation. Write an essay arguing whether more cities should do this.
text:
# Should More Cities Make Public Transportation Free?

Free public transportation is an appealing idea. Cities such as Tallinn, Estonia, and Luxembourg, which made transit free nationwide in 2020, have shown it can be done. Kansas City, Missouri, has also run free buses for several years. Still, I think most cities should not make all transit free. A better path is to make transit cheap for those who need it and to spend the saved money on better service.

## The case for free transit

The strongest argument is fairness. Poorer residents spend a larger share of their income on getting around, and many depend on buses to reach jobs, clinics, and schools. Removing fares helps them directly.

Free transit can also raise ridership. More riders can mean fewer cars on the road, less pollution, and less congestion. Boarding gets faster too, because no one has to pay at the door. In Kansas City, free fares came with a drop in the time buses spent at stops.

Fares also cost money to collect. Machines, staff, and enforcement eat up part of what a system earns. In small systems, that cost can be a large share of the revenue.

## The case against

The biggest problem is that fares pay for service. In many large cities, fares cover a major part of the operating budget. New York's subway and buses, for example, depend heavily on them. If a city drops fares, it must find that money elsewhere, usually through taxes. If it cannot, service gets cut, and riders who rely on the system end up worse off.

Research also suggests that free fares do not pull many drivers out of their cars. Studies of Tallinn found that much of the new ridership came from people who used to walk or bike. That is not a clear win for the environment or for health. Drivers tend to care more about speed, reliability, and convenience than about price.

Free service can also strain a system that is already tight. If buses are crowded and infrequent, adding riders without adding buses makes the experience worse. Some cities have also reported more disorder on free systems, which can push away riders who have other options.

Finally, free is not the same as targeted. A free system gives the same discount to a wealthy commuter and a low-income worker. Money spent that way could do more good if aimed at those who need help.

## A better approach

The goal is not free fares. The goal is a transit system that people can afford and want to use. Cities can get most of the benefits with more focused steps:

- Offer deeply discounted or free passes to low-income residents, students, seniors, and youth.
- Cap daily and monthly fares so that frequent riders never pay too much.
- Put new money into frequent, reliable service and dedicated bus lanes.
- Make free fares an option where they make sense, such as small cities with low fare revenue and spare capacity.

## Conclusion

Free transit works best in places where fares bring in little money and the system has room for more riders. For most cities, especially large ones, dropping fares entirely would take away funds that service needs. More cities should try free or nearly free transit in limited ways, but the larger priority should be building frequent, dependable service and making sure low-income riders can afford it. A bus that comes often and arrives on time is worth more than a free bus that never shows up.
